part.title: Choosing a research method

turns.text: Hi Jordan. Okay, so Professor Reyes wants our method proposal by Friday, and we still haven't picked between interviews and a questionnaire. We really need to decide today.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Yeah, I know. I've been going back and forth on it. What's your feeling?
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Honestly, I keep coming back to interviews. Everyone says they give you richer, more detailed data, and that's true. But for me the big thing is that you can follow up. If someone says they just deal with stress, you can ask them to explain what they actually mean.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Right. And people probably feel more relaxed chatting than filling in a form, too.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Hmm, I'm not so sure about that, actually. A lot of students would find it pretty awkward talking to a stranger about stress. Anyway, what about you? You were leaning toward a questionnaire, weren't you?
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: I was. I mean, obviously you can reach way more people, and the results are a lot easier to analyze. But what really convinces me is that nobody has to give their name. With a topic like exam stress, people might not admit how badly they're coping if they're sitting across from you.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: That's a fair point. And there's the time issue. Remember what Professor Reyes said in class on Tuesday? I was half expecting her to tell us our topic was too broad, but she didn't. What she did say was that transcribing and coding interviews always takes about three times longer than students plan for.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Yeah, I remember that. Though I read somewhere that online surveys get really low response rates, so questionnaires aren't exactly a quick fix either.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: True. So what if we did both? A questionnaire first, and then interviews with five or six people afterward?
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: In an ideal world, sure. But with only eight weeks, sorry, seven weeks now, I don't think we can manage it. How about this: we go with the questionnaire, but we add two or three open questions at the end, where people can answer in their own words. That way we still get some of that detail you wanted.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Okay, I can live with that. It's a good compromise. Now, who are we asking? Should we open it up to everyone, all years?
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: That's way too wide for a project this size. I did think about psychology students, since they'd be easy to find, but they'd probably guess what we're looking for, and that could skew the answers.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Good point. So let's just do first-years, and only the ones living in residence. They're all dealing with their first set of finals, and they're easy to reach.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Perfect. Okay, so let's map out the steps so we can put them in the proposal.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Right. Step one is writing the questions. I really don't want to make everything up from scratch, so I think we should adapt items from published studies. That coping scale from week three would be a good start.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Agreed. Then we need to check the wording works. I was going to try it out on my roommates, but they'd just tell us it's great. Let's test it on some classmates from the methods course instead. They'll actually be critical.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Good idea. After that, we fix anything confusing, and then it has to be approved. I assumed Professor Reyes could just sign it off, but no, anything involving human participants has to go to the ethics board.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Okay. And that can take a couple of weeks, so we should submit it early. Once it's approved, we recruit people. I asked about using the residence email list, but apparently that's only for official notices. So we'll put up flyers in each of the residence halls.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Sounds good. And for handing out the paper copies, I'd thought about the library, but they don't allow anything like that inside. So we'll set up a table in the dining hall at lunchtime. It's the busiest spot on campus, so we should get plenty of people.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Great. Then, once we've collected them all, we enter the responses into a spreadsheet. We can move everything into the statistics software later, but getting it all typed up comes first.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: And then the last step is presenting it. I'd assumed we'd do a slideshow, but Professor Reyes wants every group to make a poster and explain it to the class in the final week.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Got it. Okay, I'll start writing this up tonight and send it to you tomorrow.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Perfect. Thanks, Jordan.
turns.speaker: student_a
